newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece staggers under new wave of strikes.
newsitem.headline: Greece staggers under new wave of strikes.

text.p: Greece was hit by another wave of strikes on Tuesday with doctors, civil servants, diplomats and seamen stopping work to protest against the ruling socialists' tax-heavy 1997 budget.
Civil servants gathered near central Constitution Square to march on parliament, causing traffic chaos in the heart of the capital.
Seaman pressed on with a two-day strike, halting commercial transport and tourist ferries, and making a 20-day farmers' road blockade tougher to circumvent.
The farmers, in an increasingly bitter fight with Prime Minister Costas Simitis, vowed on Monday to press on with their blockades and to march on Athens on Thursday.
The latest wave of strikes and work stoppages coincides with the start of a five-day debate in parliament on Tuesday night on the 1997 budget.
The budget has angered workers by clamping down on state hiring, limiting wage rises for another year, levying new taxes and eliminating hundreds of tax breaks.
Simitis, who won September elections, has said the tough budget was essential to meet economic targets so Greece can join a single European currency by the year 2001.
The Federation of Greek Industries (SEB) estimated that the economy had lost $108 million so far from the farmers' blockade alone.
Almost 60 percent of those asked in compiling that figure said their market share would be damaged permanently by the road blockade which has cut the country in two, a SEB statement said.
The streets of Athens have reverberated daily with chants of groups of disgruntled workers since Simitis unveiled his budget last month.

The civil servants' strike brought much of the public sector administration to a standstill and the General Confederation of Greek Workers (GSEE) -- the biggest labour grouping -- called a three-hour solidarity stoppage for Tuesday afternoon.
Civil aviation workers, except air traffic controllers, also called an two-hour sympathy stoppage on Tuesday.
The civil servants union (ADEDY) and GSEE will rally outside the parliament in the evening when the budget debate begins. The vote on the budget is set for Saturday at midnight.

Workers have demanded better pensions, higher minimum wages and expressed outrage at heavier taxation. The socialists have boosted indirect taxes on items such as alcohol and swept away hundreds of tax exemptions.
Simitis, a taciturn pro-European economist, again rejected any concessions to the farmers' on Monday, saying the government had no more money to give.
"We cannot give away hundreds of billions of drachmas. We would lose our chances of development. We would lose our chances of social justice," he told reporters.
The farmers have posed the most serious threat to Simitis so far and his government has been concerned that any concessions to them could lead to demands by a myriad of other groups.
He again rejected direct talks until farmers lifted their blockades and, even then, only to discuss agricultural reforms, not their economic demands.
The farmers want lower fuel prices, higher price supports, lower Value Added Tax (VAT) on their equipment and rescheduling $1.3 billion in debts.
